name: Grapeseed oil

lead: Grapeseed oil is pressed from seeds left over from winemaking. It is mostly linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid found in skin lipids, with a light texture. People use it as a facial, body and massage oil, especially those with oily or breakout-prone skin who want moisture without greasiness.
Linoleic-rich oils are a common emollient choice. The sources do not report mechanistic studies of grapeseed oil on skin, and trials on skin appearance were not found.

paras: It is applied as a few drops on the face or body, used for massage, blended into hair care, or included in cosmetics. It is also a cooking oil. It is typically used as a daily lightweight moisturising oil.
Some batches have been found to contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, likely from combustion gases during seed drying. Its high polyunsaturated content makes it prone to oxidation.

angle.text: Grapeseed oil is a lightweight, linoleic-rich oil used for facial and massage use by people who want moisture without heaviness, often those with oily or breakout-prone skin. It leaves skin softer and less dry-looking.

lead: Grapeseed oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of grapes, a by-product of winemaking, with production concentrated in wine regions such as the Mediterranean.[1] It is mostly linoleic acid (about 70 percent by one estimate) followed by oleic acid, with small amounts of vitamin E and plant sterols.[1]

It is used as a light salad and cooking oil, a massage oil, and in some cosmetics and hair-care products, though the cosmetic claim is uncited in the reference source.[1] Reference sources state that, unlike the seeds, the oil contains negligible polyphenols, and that as of 2016 clinical research was too weak to show disease-risk reduction.[1] No clinical studies on skin or hair appearance were found.
infobox: Seeds of Vitis vinifera grapes (winemaking by-product)

paras: Reference sources report linoleic acid at about 69.6 percent, oleic acid about 15.8 percent, palmitic about 7 percent and stearic about 4 percent, with small amounts of vitamin E; other oils such as safflower and rice bran contain more vitamin E.[1] A study of 21 grape varieties found wide variation in oil composition, especially linoleic acid and tocopherols.[1]

Studies of edible-oil oxidation have compared grapeseed oil with other oils, and a food-science study used it in oleogels with beeswax.[2][3] Its high polyunsaturated fraction is generally associated with lower stability than monounsaturated oils.

Grapeseed oil is used in dressings, mayonnaise, baked goods and for infusing herbs, and as a massage oil and in some cosmetic and hair products.[1] Studies outside cosmetics include its use as a carrier or base in an aromatherapy trial for agitation in people with dementia, in an MRI breast phantom design, and in diet studies of dietary fat and endotoxin or glycaemic response.[4][5][6][7]

Reference sources state that the oil has occasionally been found to contain dangerous levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, likely from exposure to combustion gases when seeds are dried.[1] A 2000 study examined how processing affects PAH content in grapeseed oil.[8] A rat study reported that grapeseed oil modified diazinon-induced alterations.[9]

No studies found on grapeseed oil for skin, hair or appearance. Human studies that include it concern diet: a randomised crossover study of dietary fat and postprandial serum endotoxin,[6] and registered comparisons of dietary fats on vascular parameters (n=24) and on postprandial glucose, insulin and triglycerides (n=25).[10][11] A trial of aromatherapy for dementia-related agitation used the oil as a carrier rather than testing it.[4]
